Roman Surzhikov is the author of “Traces on the Water.” Before it, he wrote the Polari series, which, according to him, was completed roughly two years before spring 2026. He calls “Traces on the Water” the first novel set in a second world, provisionally named the “World of Wells.” The information in this article comes only from two streams in which the author answered readers’ questions: the January stream (7 January 2026) and the spring one. Everything introduced as “according to the author” comes from his own words; conjectures by the host and viewers are excluded.

Polari and other works

The author said that he has set himself the goal of creating at least two fantasy worlds. The first was Polari, which has its own wiki: Polari Wiki. The concluding book of that series is “Fantasies,” which he was still working on in 2026. He intended to write its “missing fantasy,” provisionally titled “The Surplus”; according to him, the plot was already worked out, and he planned to make the text an exclusive addition to the print edition of “Fantasies.”

According to the author, the print editions of Polari were released by the publishing operation associated with the Fantlab website, run by Alexey Lvov. He described it not as a large publishing house, but as an analytical website with a small warehouse and periodic reprints. Among other works, he mentioned “The Queen Is a Lonely Piece,” his only published novel outside Polari, which he considers weaker. Another project is “Unlucky Chris,” social science fiction with black humor set in our world. He worked on it alongside “Traces on the Water”: in early 2025, he switched between Chris and the World of Wells, and in January 2026 he hoped to finish both books in the first half of the year.

For readers coming from Polari, the author recommended starting with “Traces on the Water.” He considered the new novel more dynamic and concentrated than “Arrow, Coin, Spark.” He does not rewrite published work, except for abridging “Arrow, Coin, Spark”: he regards what he has written as part of the history of a parallel reality.

The spiral of worlds

The spiral is the sacred symbol of the world of Polari. The author explained that he imagines a metaverse in which different worlds live on different turns of the spiral: Polari occupies one turn, the world of Unlucky Chris another, and the World of Wells another. It is impossible to move physically from one world to another. He referred to a possible future setting as a world of bards, but provided no details. He does not rule out returning to Polari, but “not in the next few years”: first come Chris, the World of Wells, and possibly the world of bards. See World of Wells.

How the author writes

  • He does not write drafts: after working out the plot in his head, he immediately types a “fair copy.” He rereads the text aloud once with someone close to him and revises it. He sends the manuscript to a proofreader only before a print edition; for websites, he proofreads it himself.
  • He works no more than five hours a day. In 2026, he took on a “challenge”: 12 pages per week, roughly 600 per year. At the time of the second stream, he had not missed a single week.
  • A novel begins with an image—a world, person, or situation; the author then develops it, discusses it with someone close to him, identifies the conflict, and only afterward constructs the plot. He begins writing when he can see the entire conflict, from its beginning to its resolution.
  • He writes to quiet music without words—Enigma, Dagda, Dead Can Dance—and may play the same album ten times.
  • The author uses artificial intelligence for illustrations accompanying posts, for translating long passages into English, and for reference information about unfamiliar professions; he says that he writes the texts and details of the world himself. He discussed the realism of the autopsy attended by Alvaro (Alvaro da Silva) with AI as if with a “doctor friend.”
  • One device the author singled out: he introduces each main protagonist of “Traces” to the reader in a distinctive form. This is visible in the book: Alvaro opens it with a first-person preface; Dietrich (Dietrich von Dort) appears through a service evaluation written by his commander; and Red (Red) appears in a chapter styled as a guidebook, addressing the reader as “you.” The author clarified his priorities: plot first, then the expression of feelings, then originality of form.

The world’s languages and style

The author said that Catalia (Catalia) is built stylistically on Spanish: its language, names, and clothing. Dangar (Dangar) draws on German and German-Prussian style. Ollandia (Ollandia) is close in spirit to Poland, although its language does not appear in the novel and its names are Slavic. He stresses that “Catalia is not Spain” and “Dangar is not Prussia”: they embody two ideas of the state. The author began learning Spanish while conceiving this world; he reads at the level of wiki articles and uses dictionaries and AI. He studied German at university, up to Mittelstufe II; readers sometimes find mistakes in the German words.

Publication of “Traces on the Water”

According to the author, the novel was finished by spring 2026, while its subscription-based chapter publication was drawing to an end “by Lenin’s birthday,” around 22 April. It can be read on Litspace, Author.Today, and Litnet. New chapters appeared on Fridays and holidays, usually in the morning, and in the final month at a rate of two chapters a week. The author thanked readers for correcting typos and joked that even people afraid of unfinished books could now begin reading. Kirill Golovin narrates the novel; the audio version was promised “by the end of spring.” The author said that a print edition would not appear soon: first he would finish “Fantasies.”

Alexey Safin drew a large map of the World of Wells’ three continents; at the time of the stream, only the portion in which the first book takes place had been released, and there were plans to expand the map.

The concept and interviews

  • The three protagonists—Alvaro, Red, and Dietrich—are all men. The author admitted that he now slightly regretted not making one of them a woman: usually, at least one of his three protagonists is female. He said that he did not know why it had turned out this way.
  • In response to a complaint that everyone in his books has bad relationships, the author replied that he often depicts good, genuine love, and that “Traces on the Water” “even has a married couple who are very good, from my point of view.” He did not identify which couple he meant; the novel’s principal married couple is Fernan and Lucille Gereira.
  • Alvaro grew out of the task of examining creativity within fantasy. According to the author, the character is to some extent his alter ego, and the protagonist’s philosophy often coincides with his own; at the same time, he warns beginning writers against creating a protagonist too much like themselves.
  • He confirmed that Red’s storyline takes place before those of Dietrich and Alvaro, and that later the storylines “will come together in a certain way.” The author gave no details.
  • As he explained it, Dangar is a slave-owning empire set in a notional “X century”: steam engines, cannons, and slavery exist simultaneously. The author does not “root for” the state, but sympathizes with people: among those he likes is Master Joriksen (Fritjof Joriksen); he likes Dietrich less, but still finds him sympathetic.
  • According to him, the kaiser, patriarch, and chief magnus will appear in the second World of Wells book, rather than in “Traces”; the origins of Catalia’s and Dangar’s systems and the reasons for slavery are also reserved for it.
  • The author compared Beatriz (Beatriz) with a top student like Hermione Granger: she knows the theory but has not yet written a single book, and readers will see how she does in practice in later novels set in this world.

The book within the book (ch. 34)

In response to a viewer’s comment, the author confirmed that Alvaro is writing a book titled “Traces on the Water.”
